_comment: C++ AVAILABILITY claims — 'this needs C++N'. The revision axis for C++ is the -std level, not a rename: the old form is the SAME code under an older standard. cppreference's per-standard markers (in the acquired offline archive) are the source these are drafted from; the compilers installed here are what CONFIRM them.

claims.note: constrained algorithms arrived in C++20; the <ranges> header does not even exist before it
claims.summary: constrained algorithms (`std::ranges::sort(v)`, `<ranges>`) are C++20 — under C++17 use `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())`

claims.note: a C idiom that only became legal C++ in C++20
new:
struct P { int x; int y; };
int main(){ P p{.x = 1, .y = 2}; return p.x; }
claims.summary: `P p{.x = 1, .y = 2}` is C++20 (gcc accepts it earlier only as a GNU extension; `-pedantic-errors` refuses it)

claims.note: the spaceship operator and <compare> are C++20
claims.summary: `auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default;` and `<compare>` are C++20

claims.note: constexpr std::vector needs C++20's constexpr allocation
claims.summary: `constexpr` functions may allocate (so `constexpr std::vector`) only from C++20

claims.note: C++17. Included as a control: a claim whose OLD form is genuinely older than the rest
new:
#include <string>
int main(){ std::string s = "ab"; if (auto n = s.size(); n > 1) return 0; return 1; }
claims.summary: `if (auto n = s.size(); n > 1)` — the init-statement form is C++17

new:
#include <utility>
int main(){ auto [a, b] = std::pair{1, 2}; return a + b - 3; }
